clue.text: No fortune for 14

definitions.meaning: a trifling sum of money, nowhere near a fortune
refers to the clue at 14, a comic strip: here Charles Schulz's strip with Charlie Brown and Snoopy

explanation.surface: Someone working for a comic strip complains they are paid next to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically a paltry wage is called this; it is also the title of Schulz's famous comic strip.

clue.text: Quite right, inessential clothes

indicators.note: to clothe is to cover or wrap, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: petty means trivial, inessential

explanation.surface: A remark that frills on clothing are quite unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' is a verb here: PETTY clothes R, giving PRETTY.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb the word is a synonym for fairly or rather, as in a moderately good result.

clue.text: Waiter sportingly poking spleen with base of utensil

indicators.note: a letter poking into a word is pushed inside it

parts.note: spleen means bad temper, anger

indicators.note: in a down clue the base of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A furious diner jabs at something with the end of a fork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiter sportingly' is the definition: an angler waits patiently for a bite.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisherman spends most of the sport waiting, so in sporting terms such a person is a waiter.

clue.text: Urbane lad turned page ultimately — it's garbled

indicators.note: turned signals that the letters are turned over into a new order
ultimately points to the final letter of the word page

explanation.surface: A smooth young man flips to the last page and finds it a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Garbled text is muddled beyond sense, so it cannot be read: a near synonym.

clue.text: Wells has a problem with empty pages

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

indicators.note: an emptied word keeps only its outer letters

explanation.surface: H. G. Wells struggles to fill blank pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wells' looks like the author but means pits where liquid collects.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumps are pits or reservoirs where water or oil drains and gathers, much like wells.

clue.text: A god eating five or one helping

indicators.note: eating means taking something in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A greedy deity devours five people, or perhaps just one who is serving.
explanation.definitionFit: A consultant gives guidance, so someone offering help fits as a paraphrase.

clue.text: Where planes seen investing energy in new road, where must that road end?

indicators.note: to invest is to place inside, here putting one letter within a group
in shows where the invested letter goes
new signals the letters of road made over into a fresh order

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
the proverb says all roads lead to the Italian capital

explanation.surface: Planners spend energy on a new road and wonder where it will finish.
explanation.walkthrough: ROAD rearranged gives AROD; E goes inside to make AEROD, then the capital of Italy, where every road leads.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an airfield, the place aircraft take off and land.

clue.text: Reportedly yucky bottle

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, signalling a sound-alike word

parts.note: yucky means disgusting, vile

explanation.surface: Word has it that the contents of a bottle are disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: A small glass bottle for medicine or perfume, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Relative Arthur's dad punches — that's to the point?

indicators.note: one piece punches into another, landing inside it

parts.note: a son is a relative
Uther Pendragon was King Arthur's father in legend

explanation.surface: A family member is struck by King Arthur's father, and asks if it was pointed.
explanation.definitionFit: South is a compass point, and this adjective means towards or of that point.

clue.text: Deeper ranges, good parts for the contrabassoon, perhaps?

indicators.note: a piece that parts a word splits it, sitting inside
ranges means roams about, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: PI, short for pious, means good

explanation.surface: Lower notes and fine passages written for a deep woodwind instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ranges' rearranges the word deeper to make REEDPE, and 'parts' means the good letters split it. 'good parts' reads like musical parts for the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A contrabassoon is a double-reed wind instrument, an example of a pipe sounded by a reed.

clue.text: Interpreter of music outlines case of leading composer

indicators.note: to outline is to surround, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: the ear is what takes in and makes sense of music

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer letters

explanation.surface: A musical performer sketches the profile of a top composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Elgar was the English composer of the Enigma Variations, so the surname is an example.

clue.text: 14 to damage instrument that's cracked?

parts.note: to mar is to damage
cracked means crazy, mad
uke is short for ukulele

explanation.surface: A comic strip about wrecking a musical instrument that has split.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic strip about a huge, clumsy Great Dane is titled with this name.

clue.text: Within limits of taste, he had to bite tongue in 14

indicators.note: within places the following letters inside the bounds of another word
the limits of a word are its first and last letters
biting something means closing round it

parts.note: had shortens to 'd, giving D
Farsi is a tongue, the Persian language

explanation.surface: In a comic strip a man restrains himself, keeping within tasteful bounds.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'D bites FARSI to give HEFARSID, which sits between T and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Gary Larson's single-panel cartoon series is titled with this phrase, so it is an example.

clue.text: Fruit, cool or hot?

definitions.meaning: the red berry-like fruit of a wild rose
hot can mean currently in fashion, popular

explanation.surface: Asking whether some fruit should be served chilled or warm.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose fruit carries this name, and slang uses it for trendy, as both cool and hot can mean.

clue.text: Building a shambles when put up, gaudy stuff

indicators.note: in a down clue putting a word up turns it backwards

parts.note: a shambles is a mess
bling is showy jewellery

explanation.surface: A messy construction project ends up covered in tacky decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting something together is constructing it, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: If maybe so, not dizzy in a spin?

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the other piece

parts.note: a spin is a short drive, a car trip

indicators.note: dizzy suggests letters spun out of order

explanation.surface: A query about whether a person would avoid giddiness while going round and round.
explanation.walkthrough: If... is Steve Bell's long-running comic strip in the Guardian, so 'If maybe' means an example. 'dizzy' turns so, not into TOONS, which goes 'in' the spin.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Bell's newspaper series If... is one instance of this kind of serial comic.

clue.text: War machine, the brute out to catch leader in conflict

indicators.note: catching something holds it inside
out signals the letters put out of order
the leader in a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A savage warrior sets out to seize the commander in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: THE BRUTE rearranged gives TREBUHET, which catches C.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval siege engine that hurled stones using a counterweight, a kind of military device.

clue.text: 14 raising newspaper above competitors

indicators.note: in a down clue above means coming before
in a down clue raising a word reads it upwards, backwards

parts.note: a rag is a low-grade newspaper
the field is everyone taking part in a race

explanation.surface: A comic strip gives a newspaper a lift over its rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim Davis's strip about a lazy, lasagne-loving cat carries this title.

clue.text: Get lost in good play, with end uplifted?

indicators.note: in a down clue the final letter is lifted higher up the word

parts.note: Othello is a Shakespeare play

explanation.surface: A rude dismissal heard in a fine drama whose ending is raised up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with end uplifted' lifts the play's final letter higher in this down entry, so it lands after the T, making OTOHELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude, dismissive phrases telling someone to go away, idiomatic equivalents.

clue.text: Leave one spaced out about vote, as a mission of Nixon's era

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other
spaced out suggests the letters scattered and rearranged

parts.note: a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: An instruction to depart, dazed, after an election, from the era of Nixon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spaced out' rearranges leave one into A and OELEVEN, which go 'about' the vote.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1969 moon landing happened while Richard Nixon was US president, so it is an example.

clue.text: A king mixed food up, almost entirely in a state

indicators.note: in a down clue up reads the letters backwards

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: almost entirely means all but the final letter

parts.note: a salad is a dish of mixed food

explanation.surface: A monarch tosses a dish, nearly all of it, somewhere in a state.
explanation.walkthrough: A, K and SALA read upwards give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest US state, bought from Russia in 1867, is an example.

clue.text: Lane in 14 passes round outskirts of village in 14

indicators.note: to pass round something is to encircle it

parts.note: Lois Lane is Superman's reporter colleague in the comics

indicators.note: the outskirts of a word are its outer letters

explanation.surface: A comic-book reporter strolls round the edge of a village in a strip.
explanation.definitionFit: Kim Casali's strip of romantic one-liners, each finishing its title sentence, is called this.

clue.text: Tailless fish turns back

indicators.note: turning a word round reads it backwards
tailless means losing the last letter

parts.note: the orfe is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A fish missing its tail swims about and heads home.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phrase to and fro the second word means backwards or returning.

clue.text: Pandemonium a degree among Yorkshire city gents, perhaps?

indicators.note: among places the letters in the middle of the others

parts.note: Hull is a city and port in Yorkshire, northern England
a gents, a men's public toilet, is a loo
BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree

explanation.surface: Chaos breaks out as a graduate mixes with the menfolk of a Yorkshire city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gents, perhaps' looks like men but is a British name for a men's toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean a noisy uproar or commotion, direct synonyms.

clue.text: Failure stood leaderless between political wings

indicators.note: between puts the piece inside the pair of letters

parts.note: the left and right wings are L and R

indicators.note: leaderless means losing the first letter

parts.note: rose means stood up

explanation.surface: A flop of a candidate who stood without a leader, caught between left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fails or is beaten is a flop, a synonym.

clue.text: Held up by queen, a jocular 14

indicators.note: in a down clue held up means read upwards
by shows the letters are carried within the following words

explanation.surface: A cheerful comic strip is supported by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running Daily Mirror wartime strip about a frequently undressed heroine carried this name.

clue.text: Shout curtailed with cricketing trophy beyond English batters?

indicators.note: beyond means coming after, so the rest follows the first piece
curtailed means losing the last letter

parts.note: to yell is to shout
the Ashes is the cricket series between England and Australia

explanation.surface: A shout cut short as English batsmen win cricket's famous trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'batters' looks like cricketers, but is what bats: you bat your eyelashes.
explanation.definitionFit: These fringes are what one bats when fluttering the eyes, hence things that bat.

clue.text: Might a girl be put out?

definitions.meaning: a daughter is one's offspring or child
to put out is to publish or release

explanation.surface: Asking whether a young woman might be annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means children or descendants; the verb means to publish or distribute.

clue.text: Backing singer detailed with papers for 14

indicators.note: backing means going backwards
detailed means having the tail, the last letter, cut

parts.note: a treble is a boy soprano singer
ID means identity papers

explanation.surface: A backing vocalist provides details and paperwork for a comic strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing singer' looks like one phrase, but 'Backing' turns round TREBL + ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott Adams's office-satire strip about a hapless engineer is named this.

clue.text: 14 — are you free to erase one?

parts.note: R is text-speak for are
U is text-speak for you

indicators.note: one is I, the letter to be rubbed out

parts.note: gratis means free

explanation.surface: A cartoon asks whether you are at liberty to delete something.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nickelodeon animated series about babies was also this comic strip title.
